text: A Caesar cipher shifts every letter by one fixed amount (for example A becomes D, a shift of 3). It is monoalphabetic: the same plaintext letter always maps to the same ciphertext letter, so a frequency count cracks it quickly because E stays the most common letter and is just relabeled. A Vigenere cipher uses a repeating key of shifts instead, where position 1 shifts by the first key letter, position 2 by the second, and so on, so the same plaintext letter lands as different ciphertext depending on its position. That polyalphabetic behavior flattens the frequency signal.
title: aadhar.sh: Vigenère

text: A Caesar cipher is just a Vigenere with a one-letter key. The key J repeats into the keystream JJJJJJ, shifting every letter by the same 9, which is exactly a Caesar shift of 9, and the key JJJ is identical because it repeats into the same stream. A Caesar is the period-1 case, and a Vigenere is what you get once the key has more than one letter.
title: aadhar.sh: Vigenère

text: A Vigenere cipher uses the alphabet's order, so a keyed alphabet scrambles which shifts apply. Kryptos K1 and K2 are Vigenere on a keyed alphabet: the tableau is built on the keyword KRYPTOS, so the working alphabet becomes KRYPTOSABCDEFGHIJLMNQUVWXZ instead of A through Z. K1's running key is PALIMPSEST and K2's is ABSCISSA, and decrypting K1's ciphertext (EMUFPHZLRFAXYUSDJKZLD...) yields Sanborn's line ending in the deliberate misspelling 'the nuance of iqlusion.'
title: aadhar.sh: Vigenère

text: Kryptos K3 plays a different game from K1 and K2: it is a transposition rather than a substitution. All the letters are correct and just rearranged by a route or columnar scheme. That split between substitution (swap the letters, keep the order) and transposition (keep the letters, shuffle the order) becomes the whole game once you reach the unsolved parts.
title: aadhar.sh: Vigenère

text: A repeating Vigenere key has a period, and that period is its weakness. Kasiski spacing and the Friedman test recover the key length, after which the cipher reduces to 26 little Caesar shifts that you solve separately. An autokey kills the period because instead of repeating the keyword you extend the key with the message itself (the key first, then the plaintext), so no repeat means no period to find.
title: aadhar.sh: Vigenère

text: Cracking a Kryptos-shaped cipher with no known parameters is a search over a pipeline, because you do not know the alphabet, the key, or the order of operations. The abstract toolkit includes transposition (columnar, route, rotation, skip-reads), substitution (Vigenere and the Quagmire I through IV family, which differ in which of the plaintext, ciphertext, or key alphabets are keyed, with QIII being the Kryptos one and QIV keying all three), running keys and autokeys, plus the order of stages such as transpose-then-Vigenere or Vigenere-then-transpose. You compose a candidate pipeline, run the text through it, score the output, then crank the next combination.
title: aadhar.sh: Vigenère

text: To decode a stacked cipher pipeline, set every stage to decrypt and list the stages in the reverse of how the text was encoded. A Vigenere placed above a transposition is 'Vig first' and below it is 'Vig last,' and the two orders give different ciphertext. A transposition keeps every letter but shuffles their order, while a substitution swaps the letters but keeps their order.
title: aadhar.sh: Vigenère

text: You tell signal from noise by the statistical shape of the letters. Random polyalphabetic text reads flat, with every letter roughly equally likely, while real language reads lumpy, with E, T, and A spiking. The Index of Coincidence captures this as the chance that two random letters of the text match: English is about 0.067 and uniform random is about 0.038, so a correct monoalphabetic decrypt jumps toward 0.067 while a wrong, still-polyalphabetic candidate sits near 0.04.
title: aadhar.sh: Vigenère

text: The Vigenere cipher encrypts text with a series of interwoven Caesar shifts chosen by a repeating keyword, making it a polyalphabetic substitution where one plaintext letter can map to many ciphertext letters. Although a similar idea appeared earlier, the method was misattributed to Blaise de Vigenere in the 19th century, and for a long time it carried the nickname of the cipher no one could break before Friedrich Kasiski published a general method for breaking it in 1863.
title: Vigenère cipher (Wikipedia)

text: Kryptos is an encrypted sculpture by artist Jim Sanborn installed in 1990 on the grounds of CIA headquarters in Langley, Virginia. Its main text is divided into four sections; three of them (commonly labeled K1, K2, and K3) were solved publicly by the early 2000s, while the fourth section, K4, has remained unsolved for decades despite hints released by Sanborn.
title: Kryptos (Wikipedia)

text: The index of coincidence is the probability that two letters drawn at random from a text are the same. It is useful in cryptanalysis because it stays roughly constant under monoalphabetic substitution but drops toward the value for uniform random text under polyalphabetic encryption, which lets analysts detect a Vigenere-style cipher and estimate the key length.
title: Index of coincidence (Wikipedia)

text: Columnar transposition is a transposition cipher: it keeps every letter of the message but rearranges their order instead of substituting letters. You write the message into a grid row by row under a keyword, then read it back out one column at a time, taking the columns in the alphabetical order of the keyword's letters (ties broken left to right). The keyword KRYPTOS, for instance, ranks its seven columns 0 3 6 2 5 1 4, so you read the K column first, then O, P, R, S, T, and Y. The final row is usually ragged, so the columns differ slightly in length, and the recipient needs the keyword to rebuild the grid and reverse it. Kryptos section K3 is solved as a route transposition followed by a keyed columnar transposition, with no letter substitution at all.

Double columnar transposition runs the columnar step twice: the ciphertext from the first transposition is written into a fresh grid under a second keyword and read out by columns again. Chaining two passes scrambles the column structure far more thoroughly than one pass, and the hand-worked double transposition resisted practical cryptanalysis for decades. Because it is still a pure transposition, a letter-frequency count of the ciphertext matches the plaintext's exactly; only the positions move. That is why transposition is usually stacked with a substitution stage such as Vigenere, so the two together hide both the letters and their order.
